A retail collaborative practice agreement expressly allows initial Schedule VI prescriptions. The supervising physician referred an adult patient with hypertension, and the collaborating pharmacist issues an authorized Schedule VI antihypertensive prescription for that referred diagnosis late Friday afternoon. The physician's office will not reopen until Monday. What should the pharmacist do next?
Arrange to send a copy of the prescription to the supervising physician within 24 hours rather than waiting for the office to reopen.
Wait until Monday because the 24-hour copy requirement excludes weekends and holidays.
Keep the prescription only in the pharmacy's collaborative-practice file unless the supervising physician later requests a copy.
Send the prescription copy to the Board within 24 hours and provide it to the supervising physician at the next scheduled review.
No copy is required because the agreement already authorizes initial Schedule VI prescribing for the referred diagnosis.

An adult asks a trained Massachusetts pharmacist to prescribe a self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive. She has never previously received a contraceptive prescription. What is the most accurate response under the pharmacist-prescribing statute?
A prior prescription is mandatory before a pharmacist may use this pathway.
Lack of a prior prescription is not itself a bar; the pharmacist still must follow the required screening and protocol process.
The pharmacist may prescribe any contraceptive dosage form because the patient has no prior prescription.
The patient must first obtain a controlled-substance registration because hormonal contraception is Schedule II.
The pharmacist may skip the self-screening risk assessment when the patient is a first-time user.

A patient previously received a hormonal contraceptive prescription directly from a Massachusetts pharmacist. The applicable follow-up period has now elapsed, and the patient cannot provide the required evidence of a clinical visit. The patient asks the pharmacist to issue another prescription anyway. Which response best fits the statutory pathway?
Issue another pharmacist prescription because a prior pharmacist prescription permanently waives follow-up requirements.
Switch to an injectable contraceptive so the clinical-visit requirement no longer matters.
Do not repeat the pharmacist prescribing pathway when the required post-prescribing clinical-visit evidence is absent after the applicable period.
Treat the missing clinical-visit evidence only as an insurance problem and prescribe normally.
Have a technician override the screening record because the patient previously tolerated the medication.

A father asks a Massachusetts community pharmacy to obtain a prescription-labeled naloxone product through the pharmacy's authorized naloxone prescription/standing-order pathway because his adult daughter recently survived an opioid overdose. The daughter is not present. Which conclusion is most defensible?
The pharmacy must refuse because naloxone may be supplied only to the person at risk.
The father must first be diagnosed with opioid use disorder before he can receive naloxone.
The request must be processed as an emergency Schedule II opioid prescription.
A lawful Massachusetts naloxone pathway can include a person positioned to assist someone at risk of overdose.
Community pharmacies may provide naloxone only when an emergency department transfers the patient’s prescription.

During a shelf audit, a Massachusetts pharmacist finds two naloxone nasal-spray cartons mixed together: one is an FDA-labeled OTC package with Drug Facts, while the other is prescription-labeled and states that federal law prohibits dispensing without a prescription. Both contain naloxone. What is the most appropriate correction?
Move both cartons to prescription inventory because Massachusetts treats every naloxone product as prescription-only once it enters a pharmacy.

Keep the OTC-labeled carton available for ordinary retail sale, but return the prescription-labeled carton to prescription inventory for dispensing only through lawful prescription or standing-order authority.
Treat both cartons as OTC when their active ingredient and strength match because the FDA nonprescription status attaches to naloxone itself rather than to the labeled product.
Treat the OTC-labeled carton as prescription-only whenever a customer wants insurance billed because the payment method changes the product's legal classification.
Allow the prescription-labeled carton to be sold from the shelf without an order whenever the purchaser says the naloxone is for a person at risk of overdose.

A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a prescription for mifepristone 200 mg for medical termination of pregnancy through 10 weeks. The pharmacy is not currently certified in the Mifepristone REMS Program. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
Retail pharmacies are categorically prohibited from dispensing mifepristone, even if they become REMS-certified.
The pharmacy must satisfy the current Mifepristone REMS pharmacy-certification requirements before dispensing under this pathway.
The prescription must come from a prescriber who satisfies the current Mifepristone REMS prescriber-certification requirement.
Massachusetts Schedule VI status does not erase the separate federal product-specific REMS conditions.
The pharmacy can substitute ordinary Schedule VI transfer documentation for REMS certification because mifepristone is not federally controlled.

A patient presents a valid clozapine prescription in August 2026. A pharmacist trained under the former Clozapine REMS tells a colleague that the pharmacy cannot dispense until the patient is enrolled in the REMS and an ANC result is entered into that program. What is the current federal position?
The former REMS enrollment and ANC-verification gate remains mandatory for every clozapine dispensing.
The pharmacy may ignore any clinically significant blood-count information because removal of the REMS ended all clozapine monitoring concerns.
The pharmacy must enroll only the prescriber, while pharmacy and patient enrollment are no longer required.
FDA removed the Clozapine REMS, so REMS enrollment and REMS ANC verification are no longer federal dispensing prerequisites, although clinical monitoring remains relevant.
Clozapine became an over-the-counter drug when the REMS was removed.

At pickup, an adult patient is receiving a valid oxycodone prescription. The pharmacist confirms it is a Schedule II opioid. The patient says, 'I already keep unexpired naloxone at home, so we can skip anything else about overdose risk.' Under current Massachusetts law, which response best addresses the pharmacist's specific statutory duty tied to dispensing this oxycodone?
Skip both steps because having an opioid antagonist at home satisfies the Massachusetts dispensing requirement.
Inform the patient of the prescription opioid's potential adverse risks and offer to dispense an opioid antagonist; the patient may decline the offer.
Require the patient to accept an opioid antagonist before the Schedule II opioid may be dispensed.
Make the antagonist offer only when the opioid prescriber has separately ordered one or documented elevated overdose risk.
Make the antagonist offer only for a patient who has never previously received a Schedule II opioid.

A wholesaler receives an electronic CSOS order for oxycodone from a pharmacy. The order data are complete, but the wholesaler's validation system shows that the digital certificate used to sign the order was revoked before the order was transmitted. What should the supplier do?
Ship the order because complete line-item data are enough even when the signing certificate is invalid.
Print the electronic order and treat the printout as a valid paper DEA Form 222.
Reject the electronic order rather than fill it on the revoked certificate; the purchaser must submit a valid authorized order.
Ship half the order because a partial shipment reduces the risk created by the revoked certificate.
Hold the order until 60 days after execution, when the certificate-revocation issue no longer matters.

A Massachusetts pharmacist administers an eligible patient-specific long-acting antipsychotic under the current MH/SUD pathway. Which workflow principles are consistent with the guidance? Select all that apply.
Send the administration record to the prescriber as soon after administration as practical, as strongly encouraged by DCP guidance
Allow a cashier to perform the injection after the pharmacist verifies the prescription
Skip privacy protections because the medication treats mental illness
Use a prescribed single dose supplied in eligible single-dose packaging
Document the administration in the pharmacy's patient record

A community pharmacy receives an otherwise complete Schedule II methadone prescription that is annotated 'for pain.' During counseling, however, the patient states that the prescriber described the methadone as replacing the patient's opioid-treatment-program maintenance doses, and the pharmacy has no documented pain diagnosis or other explanation for the conflict. What is the pharmacist's best next step?
Dispense immediately because the written words 'for pain' conclusively determine the federal treatment pathway despite contradictory information
Reject every future methadone prescription from that prescriber because methadone can never be dispensed by a community pharmacy
Pause dispensing and clarify the prescription's actual medical purpose and treatment pathway with the prescriber before deciding whether ordinary Schedule II dispensing is appropriate
Change the prescription to buprenorphine because a pharmacist may substitute an OUD medication whenever the stated indication is uncertain
Rewrite the indication as OUD maintenance and dispense the prescription after documenting that the patient confirmed the intended use

A Massachusetts pharmacist completed the appropriate injection-training program and receives a valid patient-specific prescription for a repeat dose of Vivitrol in its single-dose presentation. The prescriber directs pharmacy administration, but the pharmacist's CPR certification expired last week. What is the best action under the current MH/SUD administration guidance?
Administer the dose because the medication, prescription, and repeat-dose requirements are otherwise satisfied
Administer the dose after obtaining an additional written patient consent acknowledging that CPR certification has expired
Postpone pharmacist administration until current CPR certification is restored, because current CPR certification is an administrator requirement
Administer the dose if another pharmacy employee with current CPR certification remains in the pharmacy during the injection
Administer the dose if the prescriber gives same-day verbal confirmation that the pharmacist may proceed despite the expired certification

A Massachusetts pharmacist administers a patient-specific dose of Abilify Maintena under the mental-illness administration pathway. Shortly afterward, the patient develops a severe reaction requiring emergency medical services and evaluation in an emergency department. Which follow-through actions are consistent with current Massachusetts guidance? Select all that apply.
Immediately report the adverse event to the prescriber because emergency-department treatment is one of the specified serious outcomes
Record the adverse outcome or adverse event in the pharmacy's administration record
If the event is a dispensing error or a serious adverse drug event, fulfill the pharmacist's or intern's applicable Board reporting responsibility
Delay prescriber communication until the next routine reassessment because the patient has already been transferred to emergency care
Omit the event from the pharmacy record when emergency medical services create their own clinical documentation

Every option below involves gabapentin stock at an otherwise eligible Massachusetts hospital ADD. Which stocking actions are permitted under the current technician-stocking policy? Select all that apply.
A nationally certified licensed technician uses the no-prior-pharmacist-verification Schedule VI shortcut for gabapentin.
A nationally certified licensed technician loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin under the ordinary supervised licensed-technician pathway.
A pharmacy technician trainee loads unverified gabapentin based only on a visual bottle check.
A pharmacy technician trainee loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin using required electronic validation under pharmacist direction and supervision.
A licensed non-trainee pharmacy technician loads pharmacist-verified gabapentin using electronic validation under pharmacist supervision.

A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives an ordinary outpatient methadone prescription whose stated purpose is ongoing OUD maintenance. The prescriber is not operating through the applicable OTP pathway. What is the best response?
Fill it as an ordinary Schedule II prescription because methadone prescriptions are identical regardless of indication.
Recognize that routine retail prescribing is not the ordinary federal methadone-OUD maintenance pathway and do not process it as a standard pain prescription.
Add five refills so treatment is not interrupted.
Reclassify methadone to Schedule III for this patient.
Sell an equivalent OTC methadone product instead.
Which statements correctly distinguish common federal OUD medication pathways? Select all that apply.
Buprenorphine-naloxone remains Schedule III; the naloxone component does not make the product noncontrolled
Methadone for ongoing OUD maintenance is not handled as an ordinary community-pharmacy Schedule II pain prescription outside the applicable narcotic-treatment framework
Methadone and buprenorphine are legally interchangeable simply because both can treat OUD
Buprenorphine becomes Schedule VI in Massachusetts when used for OUD
A qualifying buprenorphine Schedule III prescription for OUD can use the ordinary prescription-dispensing framework when all current prescribing requirements are met

Which products currently require a product-specific restricted-distribution or certified-pharmacy REMS pathway before routine dispensing, based on the bank's current official-source verification? Select all that apply.
Isotretinoin through iPLEDGE
Mifepristone under the Mifepristone REMS Program
Sodium oxybate through its restricted REMS distribution system
Clozapine solely because the former Clozapine REMS still requires pharmacy enrollment

A Massachusetts pharmacy technician trainee working under the direct supervision of a pharmacist is asked to answer the pharmacy telephone during a staffing crunch and take a new prescription from a prescriber's agent. Which statement is correct?
The trainee may take the prescription while under direct supervision.
The trainee may take the prescription if the pharmacist listens on a second handset.
The trainee may take the prescription if it is for a Schedule VI drug.
The trainee may not take prescriptions over the telephone.
The trainee may take the prescription after 500 hours of trainee employment.

A Massachusetts supervising physician refers a patient for collaborative drug therapy management, records the referral and the patient's consent in his own chart, and tells the collaborating pharmacist that the documentation is complete and nothing further is needed. Where must the individual referral and consent be recorded?
In the supervising physician's record alone, which is what the statute requires.
In the pharmacist's record alone, since the pharmacist delivers the service.
In whichever of the two records the professionals agree should hold them.
In the patient's record, by the pharmacist and by the supervising physician.
In a register filed with the Board, separately from the patient's record.

A Massachusetts pharmacist is mapping out what a proposed collaborative practice agreement could cover. Which activities may fall within collaborative drug therapy management as the statute defines it? Select all that apply.
Initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing the patient's drug therapy.
Collecting and reviewing the patient's history.
Obtaining and checking pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration.
Settling a diagnosis where a laboratory result plainly supports one.
Ordering and evaluating laboratory tests directly related to the drug therapy.

A Massachusetts pharmacist has completed no training programme of any kind. She proposes to dispense emergency contraception under the statewide standing order this week, and to dispense a COVID-19 drug under a standing order next week. How do the two proposals compare?
The emergency contraception dispensing may proceed; the COVID-19 drug may not.
The COVID-19 dispensing may proceed; the emergency contraception may not.
Both may proceed, because training is a professional expectation rather than a bar.
Neither may proceed, because both regimes require approved training beforehand.
Both may proceed once she notifies the Department that she intends to dispense.
A Massachusetts pharmacist is deciding which injections she may give in the pharmacy under the Department's current administration guidance. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
A long-acting injectable antipsychotic such as paliperidone palmitate is eligible.
Testosterone for gender-affirming care is eligible, in any of its salts.
Cabotegravir for prevention of HIV is eligible for administration.

A patient asks a Massachusetts community pharmacist to administer methadone for addiction treatment. The patient presents a valid prescription from a practitioner, and the pharmacist has completed injection training and holds current CPR certification. May the pharmacist administer it there?
Yes, because the pharmacist holds a valid prescription for the patient.
Yes, because the pharmacist has completed the required training and certification.
No, because that administration may occur only in a registered opioid treatment program.
No, because a pharmacist may never administer any medication for addiction treatment.

A prescription for an eligible long-acting injectable arrives at a Massachusetts pharmacy without the administration notation the Department's guidance asks prescribers to include. In the pharmacist's judgment the product is plainly intended to be given in the pharmacy rather than handed to the patient. What does the guidance call for?
The pharmacist is encouraged to contact the prescriber, and administration stays open.
The pharmacist must refuse to administer until a corrected prescription arrives.
The pharmacist must dispense the product to the patient rather than administer it.
The pharmacist must obtain the prescriber's written confirmation before proceeding.
The pharmacist must record the omission and report it to the Board within 24 hours.

A Massachusetts prescriber writes for an eligible injectable to be administered in the pharmacy, specifying a single dose with three refills. The pharmacy manager says the refills make the prescription unusable for administration because the conditions require single doses. Who is right?
The manager, because refills convert it into a course of therapy.
The manager, because each administration needs its own prescription.
The manager, unless the prescriber confirms the intent in writing.
The pharmacist, because single-dose prescribing may carry refills.
The pharmacist, because the single-dose condition governs packaging only.

A referred patient at a Massachusetts retail pharmacy has run out of a medication her supervising physician prescribed, and the physician is unreachable. The collaborating pharmacist has never dispensed this patient a different medication for the same condition. What may the pharmacist do under the retail collaborative power?
Initiate an equivalent medication for the same condition for up to 30 days.
Extend the current therapy the supervising physician prescribed by 30 days.
Extend the current therapy indefinitely until the physician can be reached.
Substitute a therapeutically similar agent and notify the physician afterwards.
Nothing, because the retail setting confers no continuation power at all.
A Massachusetts pharmacy proposes to run a walk-in clinic for a newly designated vaccine during a public health event. Which statements about what must be in place are correct? Select all that apply.

A Commissioner order authorizing the administration removes any need for a prescription.
Administration must accord with the Commissioner's order as well as a practitioner instrument.

A Massachusetts pharmacist faces a medical emergency at 2 a.m. The only prescription on hand is marked 'no substitution', the prescribed brand is not in stock, and an interchangeable product on the Massachusetts list is. The pharmacist dispenses the interchangeable product. Which statements about this dispensing are correct? Select all that apply.
A medical emergency permits filling a 'no substitution' prescription this way when the brand is out of stock.
The pharmacist's own note of the emergency completes what the regulation asks of the pharmacy.
The date, hour and nature of the emergency must be recorded on the prescription or in the pharmacy system.
The purchaser must indicate acceptance of the deviation in writing.
The deviation runs only toward the cheaper product, never toward the brand as written.

A Massachusetts pharmacist is dispensing a Schedule II opioid prescribed for a 15-year-old patient. The patient's mother is collecting the medication. The pharmacist has already explained the potential adverse risks of the opioid. What does the statute require next?
Nothing further, because a minor cannot be dispensed an opioid antagonist.
Offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the mother as the minor's parent.
Offer to dispense an opioid antagonist only if the prescriber has also ordered one.
Obtain the prescriber's authorisation before raising an opioid antagonist with the family.
Record that the patient is a minor and treat the antagonist offer as inapplicable.

A community pharmacy receives an individually signed referral for a patient to enter a collaborative drug therapy management program. The document lists the patient's name and address, primary diagnosis, authorized comorbid diagnoses, and detailed treatment instructions. It does not state the patient's known allergies and contains no statement that the patient gave written informed consent. The pharmacist notes that the affiliated hospital often begins inpatient collaborative management through a consultation request that does not contain those two items. What is the best conclusion for the community-pharmacy referral?
It is sufficient because a signed referral and specific treatment instructions replace the need for allergy and consent information.
It is sufficient if the hospital's consultation process would accept the same document.
It is incomplete because a community CDTM referral must include known allergies and a statement of written informed consent, in addition to the other required patient-specific information.
It is incomplete only if the patient has a known allergy that would change the treatment instructions.
It may be completed by treating the hospital's consultation request as an incorporated attachment, even though that request contains neither missing item.
